parole.significato: abelmosk (Abelmoschus moschatus, an evergreen shrub of the East and West Indies and Northern Africa)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin abelmoschus, from Arabic حَبّ الْمِسْك (ḥabb al-misk, “pills of musk”).

parole.significato: alkanet (Alkanna tinctoria, a plant whose root is used as a red dye)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin alcanna, from Arabic الحِنَّاء (al-ḥinnāʔ).

parole.significato: place (numeric: the column counting a certain quantity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin algorismus, a transliteration of the Arabic form of the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwārizmī. Doublet of algoritmo. Cognate with Spanish guarismo.

From Old Galician-Portuguese almirante, from Medieval Latin amiratus under influence from -ante and Arabic ال (al-, “the, of the”), from Byzantine Greek ἀμιράς (amirás), from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander”). See Spanish almirante, French amiral, and English admiral.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin antimonium.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese azur (“blue”), a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lazulum, borrowed from Arabic لََازُوَرْد (laāzuward). Doublet of azur, from French. Compare with Galician azul (“blue”), Spanish azul (“blue”), French azur (“azure”), Italian azzurro (“blue”) and English a

From Latin baiulāre (“to carry a burden”) or perhaps from Arabic بَجُلَ (bajula, “to be worshipped”).

parole.significato: coat hanger (device, in the shape of shoulders, used to hang up coats, shirts, etc.)
parole.testo: Uncertain origin. Possible origins include: * Latin capitulum; * Arabic مَقْبِض (maqbiḍ, “handle”), with the ma- being confused with the Portuguese feminine indefinite article uma; * Arabic قَابِض (qābiḍ, “tongs, clamp”); * cavidado, past participle of cavidar (“to protect”), with the suggestion tha
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cifra (“zero, numeral”), from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, empty, nothing”). Doublet of zero.

parole.significato: dura mater (outermost layer of the meninges)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dūra māter [cerebrī] (literally “hard mother [of the brain]”), loan translation of Arabic أُمّ الدِّمَاغ الصَفِيقَة (ʔumm ad-dimāḡ aṣ-ṣafīqa, literally “thick mother of the brain, matrix of the brain”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin scaccum, from Arabic شَاه (šāh, “shah; king in chess”).
Learned borrowing from Latin genius. The sense of genie is also a phono-semantic matching of Arabic جِنِّيّ (jinniyy) (compare French génie).

From Old Galician-Portuguese matar, probably from Latin mactāre (through Vulgar Latin *mattāre). The development of -ct- would be irregular, however. From meco (“dissolute man”) + trefe (“mischievous”), first element from Latin moechus (“adulterer, fornicator”), second element of unknown origin. Or, possibly of shared origin with Spanish mequetrefe by borrowing from Arabic مُخَطْرِف (muḵaṭrif, “raving”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ).
From Latin resalgar, from Arabic رَهْج اَلْغَار (rahj al-ḡār, literally “cave dust”).
From Medieval Latin saphena, from Arabic صَافِن (ṣāfin), from Hebrew צֹפֵן (ṣōfēn, “hiding”).
From Medieval Latin tamarindus, from Arabic تَمْر هِنْدِيّ (tamr hindiyy).

Unknown. Possibly from: * Vulgar Latin *amidum, from Latin amylum (“starch”); * Arabic خَمَّجَ (ḵammaja, “to rot”); * Arabic اَلمُخّ (al-muḵḵ, “the marrow”). Cognate with Spanish hámago, Galician ámago and Catalan àmec.
